processing: Fully oxidised Ceylon black tea, sold in OP and BOP grades.
harvest_season: Year-round. Nuwara Eliya teas are generally most prized from the dry months early in the year.
appearance_dry: Dark, wiry leaf with some brown tones, as is usual for high-grown OP.
appearance_liquor: Light, bright amber, as is typical of Nuwara Eliya.
appearance_wet: Coppery leaf with some greener edges.
taste_profile: As with other Nuwara Eliya teas, expect a light, bright and delicately floral cup with a crisp finish.

brewing.notes: Western style. Slightly cooler water and a shorter steep keep it from turning sharp. Best without milk.

vintage_note: Sold by estate and grade through merchants, not by vintage. Drink within a year or so, since the delicate aroma is first to fade. Ask for lots from the early-year quality season, as with other Nuwara Eliya estates.
description:
Lover's Leap is a tea estate close to Nuwara Eliya town, about 3.5 km away, at more than 6,000 ft by one seller's account. Its name is tied to a legend about the waterfall on its land.

It makes ordinary-process black tea in OP and BOP grades. At this height, leaf grows slowly, and as with other Nuwara Eliya teas that tends to mean a lighter, more aromatic cup than the Ceylon most people know.

Brew it a little cooler and shorter than a lowland tea, and skip the milk. It is meant to be bright and floral rather than strong.

You will find it from several Western merchants under the estate name. Royal stories in the marketing, such as service at Jubilee events, are hard to check, so judge it by the grade and freshness.
history:
The story is mostly folklore. In the legend, a prince and a commoner forbidden to marry leapt to their deaths at the waterfall.

The estate is said to date from the late 19th century, and one guide treats it as part of the wider Pedro estate complex established in 1885. A claim that James Taylor owned it has little behind it.
